en: Abhidhānottara, Chapter 45: The Consecration and Ritual Preparation for Paintings and Images.
[1426] Furthermore, I shall now describe the characteristics of images and paintings.
A wise person should maintain an image made of great conch-shell.
One should always wear [an image] that is complete with all the marks and possesses the most excellent limbs and members;
one should smear it with feces and urine, and likewise with blood and semen.
The beginner practitioner should worship with human flesh;
he attains the unsurpassed state by worshipping himself.
... he shall obtain the glorious [state] born of the [mantra].
In accordance with one’s karma, one may become an elephant or a horse;
having painted a great leather-cloth [mandala], one should accomplish the practice—
there is no need for hesitation in this matter.

Through the Yoginī on the Guru’s festival day, and likewise through the Ḍākinī born of the sacred seats (pīṭha), those who have this as their mouth shall obtain [the goal]. Having worshipped the Guru for a very long time, one should perform the worship of the Guru constantly.
For the *ḍākinī*sādhana, one should paint the cloth on elephant hide.
For the [yoginī] sādhana, one should paint it on [goat] hide.
For the *khecarī*sādhana, one should paint the cloth on horse hide.
In the sādhana of the Bhūcarī, one should paint the cloth-scroll on buffalo hide;
[in the sādhana of the Khecarī, one should paint it] on boar hide;
in the sādhana of the Yakṣiṇī, one should paint the cloth-scroll on a plank of *vaṭa* wood.
In the sādhana of an *apsaras*, one should paint the cloth on a panel of *campaka* wood;
[in the sādhana of a *keśarī*,] one should paint it on a panel of *keśara* wood. In the sādhana of a human woman (*mānuṣī*), one should paint the cloth on a rag from a cremation ground.
For the accomplishment of the doctrines of other schools, one should paint the cloth on donkey skin;
for [other purposes], one should paint it on human skin;
for the summoning of liquor, one should paint the cloth on monkey skin.
For the summoning of blood, one should draw [the deity] upon a skull.
For the summoning of semen...
[and so forth]. For the summoning of gods, one should draw the cloth-painting on a plank of *devadāru* wood.
In the practice for subduing a city, one should paint the cloth on the skin of a jackal;
[in the case of] pacification, one should paint the cloth on a red rag. For the rite of enrichment (*pauṣṭika*), one should paint the cloth on a rag from a *kṣatriṇī* (a woman of the warrior caste).
[for] the rite of exorcism, one should paint the cloth on a rag from a *ḍomba* or a washerman;
for the rite of immobilization, having drawn a banner, and likewise for immobilization...
Furthermore,
having drawn two lions upon a piece of royal hide, one should perform the summoning (*ākarṣaṇa*); this [rite] accomplishes all activities.
Furthermore, various other rites are accomplished through recollection.
For the purpose of pacifying obstacles, one should draw [the deity] upon a hare skin;
and for the purpose of producing obstacles, one should draw [it] upon a palanquin skin.
O best of lions, [the image] should especially be fashioned from gold, silver, and so forth, or from copper, crystal, lapis lazuli (rājāvartaka),
or emerald; likewise from sandalwood, deodar (devadāru), red sandalwood, and campaka.
The *aśoka* tree grants success, while the *śrīvṛkṣa* bestows wealth;
specifically, with *agaru*, *aṅkoṭa*, or milk-exuding trees,
the accomplishment of the *yakṣa* is achieved on a rag or on birch-bark.
One should fashion [the image] from tortoise bone, especially on a nāga-tree;
from tortoise bone or elephant tusks, especially for a market-place in the rainy season;
and with the bone of Brahmā for rites of pacification (śāntika), while an elephant tusk is used for rites of nourishment (pauṣṭika).
For subjugation (*vaśya*), [use] the bone of a horse; for killing (*māraṇa*), the bone of a buffalo;

for expulsion (*uccāṭana*), the bone of a camel; for creating enmity (*vidveṣa*), the bones of both a horse and a buffalo; for paralyzing (*stambhana*), one’s own bone; and for attracting (*ākarṣaṇa*), the bone of a lion.
And for going to the netherworld (pātāla), one should fashion [the image] from the bones of a boar; for rites of pacification (śāntika), it should always be made with white clay;
for rites of enrichment (pauṣṭika) with yellow clay, and for rites of subjugation (vaśya) with red clay.
For killing, black earth [is used];
such, in brief, is the ritual procedure.
One should combine feces, urine, fat, and blood with great lampblack,
and rub it together with human bone while adding the pigments.
One should also add semen from a *svayambhū* flower, or from a *ḍombikā*, or a Brāhmaṇī woman.
Whether from a Mātaṅgī, a Pukkāsī, a Rajakī, or a Vaṭakī;
or even from one's own mother, sister, or especially a daughter— from these women, having gathered the most excellent jewels of semen, [one should proceed].
Having painted the cloth according to the rules and the prescribed ritual by mixing these [pigments],
one should prepare the supreme cloth using a brush made from the hair of a corpse,
and one should weave the thread using the hair of a corpse. This is the supreme cloth.

Having perfumed the discarded offerings of the hungry ghosts (preta-nirmālya), one should offer a lamp with human fat. One should incense it with human flesh and present marrow as the sacrificial food (naivedya).
With the feces and semen, which are fragrant, and with the skulls of men, one should offer libations.

One should cause the *argha* vessel, skull-cups, *argha* water, powdered bones, and sacrificial offerings (*pasava*) to be presented with effort, according to one's ability and in accordance with the ritual practice. Furthermore, there are two kinds of mudrās, which are endowed with both wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*).
The wise one should have an image or a cloth-painting (paṭa) made according to the prescribed rite, in accordance with the ritual action, [depicting him] wearing garments and forms;
[he should be depicted] with loose hair, etc., possessing the color and intellect [of the deity].
Artisans, yogins, and likewise teachers should remain engaged with their mudrās during the consumption of feces, urine, and meat;
they should recite [the mantra] with a concentrated mind, especially while using colored pigments.
Through dances, songs, offerings, meals, and the finest drinks,
one should carry out the sequence of rites until completion;
at the time of the consecration, the preparations should be doubled.
One should offer special items such as waist-bands, anklets, and armlets;
sandals with a single toe-ring, a head-ornament, a parasol, and fly-whisks;
likewise, various animals and diverse, excellent meats.
In various occasions for drinking wine, there is the highest of all; among the finest essences of diverse flavors, there is the most excellent flower;
and amidst the clamor of musical instruments, there are the most sublime and divine courtesans.

One should especially provide the assembly of disciples with the seal of the Ācārya; likewise, in the offerings of bali and upahāra, with the finest incense and perfumes, with various kinds of king-incense, and especially with garlands of lamps. [145]
It is indeed covered with a canopy, adorned with mirrors and chowries,
fashioned with necklaces and half-necklaces, and decorated with garlands of cloth and flowers;
it is filled with pairs of garments and with skulls containing the nectar of primordial wisdom.
One should offer the five precious medicinal herbs and especially fragrant incense,
using specific vessels for the *argha* offering, along with mango sprouts,
lotuses, *āmla*, *jambu*, *kadamba*, *bilva* fruits, and *bījapūraka* fruits.
Balāmoṭā, Kṛtāñjali, Girikarṇikā, Ekavīrā, and Sahadevā— these five are known as the medicinal herbs (auṣadhī).
All these herbs should be prepared, and the wise man should pour them into the pitcher.
[He should offer] golden *jātiphala* fruits, or even the fruit of the *yugapsā*;
a golden sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), a cloth seal (*paṭamudrā*) adorning the body;
all the naked female practitioners (*susādhakī*), singing auspicious songs.
One should perform noble and manifold offerings without conceptualization toward a practitioner of pure mind whose heart is devoted and focused with faith.
The forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Consecration and Ritual Infusion for the Rite of Cloth Paintings and Images," from the *Abhidhānottarottara*.
